item.text: {"question_id":"4B.3","answer":"In 2023, formal legal protections for expression, press freedom, assembly, association, information access, and internet access remained, and independent media, online mobilization, opposition demonstrations, and civil-society monitoring continued. The Supreme Court invalidated López Obrador’s Plan B reforms, while domestic and international rights groups generally operated without restriction and officials were often cooperative. These conditions show meaningful civic space, but not consistently protected civic freedom. López Obrador and his administration publicly stigmatized journalists, NGOs, defenders, protesters, and judges; presidential-conference rhetoric was associated with documented attacks and online abuse. ARTICLE 19 recorded 561 press aggressions, identifying the Mexican state as the largest identified aggressor, including federal-authority cases, while press violence, self-censorship, protest criminalization, excessive force, arbitrary detention, surveillance concerns, and impunity persisted. The administration’s rhetoric, public-authority conduct, protection-system shortcomings, and failure to ensure diligent investigation are attributable at the executive or state-institutional level, but individual killings, criminal attacks, and many local abuses cannot be attributed personally to López Obrador on the supplied evidence. There is contrary evidence of protection mechanisms, increased staffing, shelters, victim support, UN cooperation, and other human-rights initiatives, but these measures did not establish that violations were broadly remedied.","supporting_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E014","BATCH-0004-E015","BATCH-0003-E012","BATCH-0012-E007","BATCH-0012-E008","BATCH-0012-E009","BATCH-0014-E005","BATCH-0026-E017","BATCH-0026-E018","BATCH-0029-E006","BATCH-0041-E006","BATCH-0051-E008","BATCH-0031-E010"],"contrary_or_qualifying_evidence_ids":["BATCH-0004-E015","BATCH-0015-E018","BATCH-0052-E011","BATCH-0014-E001","BATCH-0026-E016","BATCH-0026-E017"],"limitations_and_gaps":["The supplied evidence does not provide a complete national account of remedies for every 2023 violation.","Many physical attacks, killings, surveillance incidents, and local-government abuses lack an established personal causal link to López Obrador.","Some favorable institutional measures involve federal, state, local, UN, civil-society, or independent-judicial actors and cannot be attributed solely to the ruler.","Some evidence spans 2022 or extends into 2024; it is used only as explicitly identified context or for retrospective assessment of continuing patterns.","ARTICLE 19’s documented totals may undercount violence, and its organizational conclusions are not equivalent to judicial findings."],"corrections_made":["Removed the unsupported implication that independent media operation and internet access demonstrated administration protection or remedy.","Added the omitted evidence that the Mexican state was the largest identified aggressor, that public-authority attacks included federal conduct, and that press-violence networks were not meaningfully dismantled or held accountable.","Specified the documented link between presidential-conference rhetoric and attacks without treating it as proof that López Obrador ordered private or criminal violence.","Preserved contrary evidence of rights-group operation, UN cooperation, protection-mechanism staffing, shelters, victim support, and other institutional initiatives while limiting their attribution and remedial significance.","Added the Plan B demonstrations and Supreme Court invalidation as evidence that opposition mobilization and an independent check remained practically available, without converting that fact into voluntary presidential protection."],"reasons_to_reopen_full_ledger":["Reopen if the full ledger contains more direct evidence on López Obrador’s response to individual attacks, protest violations, surveillance allegations, or protection-mechanism outcomes.","Reopen if additional 2023 evidence materially changes the balance between federal executive conduct, subnational authorities, criminal groups, and independent institutions."]}
